title: Tortilla Chips 300g

drivers.name: Store closure (Monday)
drivers.evidence: One-day closure in a 7-day week; past closure in same store (2026-09-05) saw 12% drop in sales. Shrink effect due to low evidence count.

drivers.name: Price increase (+3.7%)
drivers.evidence: Two recent weeks at $3.97: median x0.73 vs baseline. Price elasticity implied; noise-adjusted effect shrunk to -15%.

adjustment.analysis: The store closure on Monday (2026-10-19) reduces the selling days by 1/7, likely lowering sales by ~14%. The price increase to $3.97 (+3.7%) is above the regular $3.83, which historically correlates with lower demand: the two recent weeks at this price saw 75 and 106 units (x0.61 and x0.85 vs baseline). Combined, these drivers suggest a downward adjustment. The classical model’s 1.00 multiplier ignores the closure and price effect. Evidence is strong for both drivers, but the closure effect is estimated from a single past occurrence (store closure), so shrink toward 1.0. The price effect is supported by two recent observations.

KNOWN PLAN FOR THE TARGET WEEK:
  events: none
  shelf price: 3.97 (+3.7% vs regular price 3.83)
  planner notes: Store closed Monday for renovation

STATISTICAL BASELINE (exponential smoothing of recent sales; it ignores events, promotions and prices):
  median 124.2 | 5%-95%: 77.7 - 200.1 | 10%-90%: 89.1 - 170.1

In the evidence below, 'vs baseline' = actual units / what this same baseline predicted for that week.
It is the multiplier that would have been right, so it maps directly onto median_multiplier.
This product's ordinary weeks already swing about +/-29% around the baseline, so a past effect smaller than that, seen only a few times, is mostly noise. The
'noise-adjusted estimate' is the effect shrunk toward x1.0 for that noise and the number of sightings.
